authorship: Assistant-authored after reading each complete source chapter; not human gold or model replay.
split: TRAIN only; never model-visible in evaluation.

bullets: The Time Traveller argues that real objects extend through duration as well as three spatial dimensions, treating time as a fourth dimension rather than an entirely separate kind of thing.
He proposes that people might eventually accelerate, stop or reverse their passage through time, using movement in space and vivid recollection as analogies; his guests challenge the possibility.
The group imagines historical visits and future investment opportunities, but these are proposed uses of a machine, not journeys that have already happened.
Claiming experimental verification, the Time Traveller goes to his laboratory and returns while the guests suspect a conjuring trick; the chapter ends before the demonstration.
review_points: Attribute the dimensional theory and possible travel to the speaker.
Do not import the model's disappearance from Chapter II or a later journey.

bullets: In a brightly lit room under close observation, the Psychologist presses the lever of the Time Traveller's miniature machine, which briefly blurs and then vanishes from the table.
The Time Traveller attributes the disappearance to travel through time, but says he does not know whether the model has gone into the future or the past.
Guests question why a machine travelling through their time would be invisible; the Psychologist proposes that rapid passage makes its impression too brief to perceive.
The Time Traveller shows them a nearly finished full-sized machine in his laboratory and declares his intention to explore time himself.
The narrator finds trickery difficult to explain, while the others recall earlier illusions and remain puzzled and sceptical rather than clearly convinced.
review_points: Distinguish the witnessed disappearance from the proposed time-travel explanation.
The full-sized machine is unfinished and its human journey is still intended.
Destination of the miniature is explicitly uncertain.

bullets: The narrator and earlier guests remain sceptical of the machine, partly because the inventor's ingenuity makes his demonstrations seem like tricks.
At the following Thursday's dinner, the absent host returns dirty, pale, injured and limping in blood-stained socks, then washes, changes and eats ravenously before explaining himself.
The newer guests ridicule time travel, while the narrator and others connect his extraordinary condition with the earlier demonstration; the cause has not yet been narrated.
The Time Traveller says he has experienced eight days since that afternoon and agrees to recount what happened only if the guests will listen without interruption; his detailed account follows.
review_points: Preserve observed injuries separately from the speaker's eight-day claim.
Do not supply the still-untold future adventure.
Dinner occurs the following Thursday, not eight ordinary days after the previous meeting.

bullets: The Time Traveller recounts completing his machine that morning and testing it: an apparently momentary movement advances the laboratory clock from about ten to half-past three.
Accelerating further, he sees days and seasons race past and buildings and vegetation change, while unpleasant motion gives way to exhilaration, curiosity and fear.
He worries that stopping inside solid matter could cause a catastrophic collision, but abruptly brakes anyway and is thrown beside the overturned machine into a hailstorm.
Near a great white sphinx and unfamiliar buildings, he fears what humanity may have become and struggles to right the machine so that he can escape.
With retreat possible, his confidence returns; he sees robed figures and an approaching small, graceful, frail person, then takes his hands off the machine. The chapter ends at this first encounter.
review_points: Present feared collision and hostile future humans as possibilities, not events.
Do not invent a destination year, the name Eloi, their society, or the machine's later disappearance.
Keep initial clock test, acceleration, abrupt arrival and first encounter in order.

bullets: A secretive old seaman settles at the Admiral Benbow inn with a sea-chest, spending his days watching the coast and his evenings drinking rum.
He tries to avoid other sailors and pays the narrator to watch for a seafaring man with one leg, whose imagined appearances then haunt the boy's dreams.
The captain bullies customers into listening to songs and violent stories, yet some enjoy the excitement; his prolonged stay without further payment frightens and burdens the narrator's father.
When the captain threatens Dr. Livesey with a knife, the doctor calmly invokes his authority as a magistrate. The captain backs down and remains quiet for several evenings.
review_points: The one-legged sailor is feared and imagined, not yet encountered.
Do not reveal the sea-chest's contents or later identities.
Nobody has seen the sea-chest open; the chapter does not establish that it is locked.
Distinguish fear of losing customers from the narrator's belief that some enjoyed the visitor.

bullets: A stranger missing two fingers questions Jim and waits for the captain, whom he calls Bill. The frightened captain recognises him as his old shipmate Black Dog.
Their private conversation turns into a cutlass fight; Black Dog flees with a wounded shoulder after the inn's signboard intercepts the captain's final blow.
Back inside, the captain demands rum and collapses. Jim and his mother fear a battle wound, but Dr. Livesey identifies a stroke rather than an injury from the fight.
After treating him and helping him upstairs, the doctor warns that continued drinking could kill him and says he should rest for a week; the captain is alive at the chapter's end.
review_points: Black Dog escapes; he is not killed.
The captain's collapse is a stroke in the narrative, not a cutlass wound.
Do not import the captain's death from the next chapter.

bullets: The weakened captain pressures Jim into bringing one glass of rum despite the doctor's warning, then finds himself too weak to carry out his plan to leave.
He says he was Flint's first mate and that former crewmates want his sea-chest, instructing Jim to summon Dr. Livesey and the authorities if specified pursuers or the black spot appear.
Jim's father dies that evening, and mourning and inn duties push the captain's confidences aside; the captain resumes drinking but continues to weaken.
After the funeral, a threatening blind visitor forces Jim to lead him to the captain and passes the captain a summons. Seeing its deadline, the captain rises, collapses and dies of another stroke.
review_points: Keep the father's death distinct from the captain's later death.
The blind visitor is not named in this chapter.
The sea-chest's sought contents remain unspecified; do not insert a discovered map.
The black spot is a summons, not a weapon that physically kills the captain.

bullets: Jim and his mother seek help after the captain's death. Frightened neighbours refuse to defend the inn, but supply a pistol, promise horses and send a boy for the doctor.
Returning to recover the unpaid lodging money, they find the black spot's ten-o'clock deadline, take the key from the captain's neck and open his sea-chest.
Among the contents are money and an oilskin packet. Jim's mother insists on counting only what she is owed, even after the blind man's return warns them of danger.

A distant whistle finally makes them leave with the money already counted and the packet. As pursuers approach, Jim's mother faints, and he drags her partly under a bridge, where they remain exposed and near the inn.
review_points: The neighbours provide limited assistance, not none.
The packet is not opened or identified as a treasure map in this chapter.
The mother does not finish collecting the exact debt or take the whole bag.
Their flight ends at the bridge, not in safety at the hamlet.

bullets: The narrator dreams of Lineland, whose inhabitants move along one straight line; a being he initially mistakes for a woman identifies himself as its king.
The king regards his line as the whole of space and cannot conceive of anything outside it, interpreting the visitor only through his own limited experience.
All inhabitants look like points from within the line and cannot pass one another, so neighbours remain fixed; voices distinguish the line-shaped men from the point-shaped women.
The king explains an imagined society in which distant partners marry and produce children through harmonising voices, with repeated weekly choruses gradually bringing unmatched voices into accord.
review_points: This visit is explicitly a dream, not a physical journey.
The king's account describes fictional Lineland, not real biological reproduction.
Keep restricted sight, movement and hearing distinct.

bullets: The King of Lineland says hearing reveals people's size and position, whereas touching is forbidden; he dismisses the visitor's suggested deception as impossible.
The visitor tries to explain a plane and sideways motion beyond the king's single line, but the king cannot connect those directions with his own experience.
Leaving Lineland makes the visitor vanish from the king's sight; describing neighbouring inhabitants and then returning still fails to convince the king that another dimension exists.
The king calls the demonstration magic rather than evidence of a wider world. Their argument becomes threatening, until the narrator wakes to the breakfast bell in Flatland.
review_points: The demonstration fails to persuade; do not reverse its outcome.
Vanishing is departure from the line within a dream, not actual death.
The final bell ends the dream, not an attack successfully carried out.

bullets: On the last evening of the millennium, the narrator remembers his grandson asking what third powers mean geometrically, extending the pattern from moving points and lines to moving a square.
Insisting that geometry has only two dimensions, the narrator dismisses the suggestion, though it continues to trouble him.
A mysterious presence answers that the grandson is not foolish. An unexpected figure appears in the house, changing size in ways the narrator cannot reconcile with a familiar regular shape.

After initially mistaking the visitor for a woman, the narrator's wife finds no angles by touch and treats him as a distinguished Circle; she withdraws so he can speak privately as the new millennium begins.
review_points: The narrator presents this visit as fact within the story, unlike the preceding dream.
The visitor's full explanation is still to come.
The plain-text source's flattened exponents are interpreted through its explicit discussion of squaring and third powers, not as the integers 32 and 33.

bullets: The narrator examines the visitor as a perfect Circle, but resists his claim to come from three-dimensional Spaceland, repeatedly interpreting unfamiliar directions in two-dimensional terms.
The visitor identifies himself as a Sphere and explains that Flatland can show only his circular cross-sections, just as Lineland could show only a slice of the narrator.
He demonstrates shrinking, vanishing and returning as he moves through the plane, yet the narrator sees the changes without understanding their cause and suspects conjuring.
Using the progression from point to line to square, the Sphere argues for a cube with eight vertices and six faces; the narrator still rejects the explanation and attacks him.
review_points: Do not make the narrator convinced by the cross-section demonstration or analogy.
The text frames the Sphere's visit as real within the fictional story.
Do not import the narrator's later movement into Spaceland.
Physical change in apparent section is not a change of the Sphere's actual identity.

bullets: The chapter distinguishes passing thoughts, imaginative stories and unexamined beliefs from reflection: a connected inquiry that carefully considers a belief's supporting grounds and further consequences.

Reflection treats something observed as possible evidence for something not directly observed, rather than merely allowing one image to suggest another; an inference initially retains an element of uncertainty.
A genuine difficulty or doubt starts inquiry and gives it direction. The particular problem determines which proposed explanations and additional observations are relevant.
Past experience supplies possible solutions, but accepting the first plausible suggestion is not enough. Reflective thinking suspends judgment while seeking evidence that can confirm or refute it.
review_points: Keep imaginative coherence distinct from an intention to establish factual belief.
Neither suggestion nor inference alone guarantees truth.
Inquiry needs a particular difficulty and relevant prior experience, not merely a general instruction to think.
The chapter's Columbus illustration is not needed to convey its argument; do not repeat its historical claim as independently established fact.

bullets: The chapter argues that thought makes deliberate action and foresight possible: present things can indicate absent or future conditions, while deliberately created signs and devices extend that capacity and enrich objects with meaning.

Inference also risks error because it goes beyond what is directly known. Everyday consequences discipline some judgments, but practical skill or natural intelligence does not prevent mistaken beliefs in other domains.
Drawing on Bacon and Locke, the chapter identifies personal bias, passion, narrow experience, unquestioned authority and social habits as sources of error that education must address.

Reliable inquiry requires regulating both observation and the acceptance of suggestions. When direct testing is unavailable, people should distinguish tested evidence from untested belief and limit their confidence accordingly.
Education should cultivate lasting habits of open-minded examination and problem-appropriate reasoning, not merely transmit information or attempt to prove every statement.
review_points: Attribute the account of thought's value to the chapter rather than endorsing every historical claim about animals or societies.
Ordinary experience provides some discipline, but not sufficient general protection against error.
Testing every inference is qualified as sometimes impossible; calibrated assent remains important.
The educational conclusion concerns habits of inquiry, not encyclopedic knowledge or automatic obedience.

bullets: Training thought must direct capacities learners already possess, not create thinking from nothing. Teachers therefore need to understand individual habits and foster the learner's own activity.

Curiosity supplies material for thought, developing from physical exploration and social questioning into sustained interest in problems. Teaching should protect this existing impulse from routine, dogmatism, overstimulation and trivial distractions.

Suggestions differ in speed, variety and depth; quick answers do not necessarily show deeper thought, nor slow schoolwork lack of ability. Any subject can develop intelligence when it stimulates meaningful inquiry suited to the learner.
Orderly reflection combines varied, flexible suggestions with a steady direction toward a conclusion, avoiding both scattered ideas and rigid routine.

Purposeful activity can organize thinking through the demands and results of action. Children's activities should suit their development, prepare for adult responsibilities and build observation and inference, rather than being rejected or assumed automatically educational.
review_points: Natural thinking capacities exist before their disciplined use is taught.
The chapter does not equate every childhood question with a scientific inquiry.
Balance in suggestions matters: neither maximal speed nor maximal quantity is the universal goal.
The argument supports selected purposeful activities, not all physical activity indiscriminately or premature imitation of specialized adult work.

bullets: The chapter rejects training thought as a separate mental faculty through privileged subjects or fixed exercises. Teaching should instead arrange conditions that develop each learner's observation, curiosity and investigation.

The whole school environment shapes thinking, including teachers' unnoticed habits. Personal influence can encourage inquiry, but can also make pupils imitate the teacher, seek approval or depend on personality rather than engage with the subject.

Different studies have different dangers: abstract reasoning may become detached from life, skill practice mechanical, and informational learning an accumulation of unused facts. Skills and knowledge should be acquired through intelligent engagement with problems.

Judging education mainly by correct recitations, measurable products or outward conformity can neglect the habits that produce them. Inquiry and deliberation in significant questions of conduct also shape wider intellectual attitudes.
review_points: The chapter distinguishes acquiring information from using it wisely; it does not claim thought needs no factual knowledge.
Teacher influence includes stimulus and response, not imitation alone.
The three groups of studies overlap; their dangers are tendencies, not inevitable outcomes.
Do not turn criticism of mechanical drill or external standards into rejection of all practice, correct answers or moral rules.

bullets: The chapter uses logical thinking chiefly to mean careful, thorough and orderly reflection suited to circumstances, rather than either any conclusion-producing thought or only formally necessary proof.

It rejects a shared assumption behind opposing educational approaches: that natural interests and logical development are separate. Neither spontaneous activity without intellectual guidance nor imposing ready-made classifications adequately trains thought.

Organized subject knowledge represents an achievement of the trained mind, not a starting point learners can simply copy. Education should develop existing curiosity, inference and testing into deliberate, dependable inquiry.
Genuine discipline is the capacity for independent mental control, and thus supports freedom. Mechanical drill may secure uniform conduct without cultivating that capacity.

Meaningful activities naturally encounter difficulties that stimulate reflection. Thoughtful habits must develop from childhood through working on such problems, rather than waiting for reasoning to appear automatically in adolescence or treating freedom as unchecked impulse.
review_points: The psychological and logical are connected stages of development, not opposing faculties.
The chapter criticizes using adult classifications as an imposed starting point, not the eventual value of organized knowledge.
Obstacles within meaningful activity are distinguished from arbitrary tasks imposed merely to create difficulty.
Discipline is not rejected; it is defined positively as independent intellectual power.

bullets: Examples of choosing a route, explaining a ferryboat pole and investigating soap bubbles show a common reflective process across practical decisions, everyday observation and scientific experiment.

The chapter distinguishes five elements: encountering a difficulty, defining it, suggesting a solution, reasoning through its implications, and testing it through further observation or experiment; the first two may merge.
Carefully identifying the problem and considering alternative explanations help prevent premature conclusions. A proposed solution goes beyond observed facts and should initially remain tentative.

Reasoning develops a hypothesis's consequences; observation or deliberately arranged experiments then test them against facts and rival explanations. Even a strongly supported conclusion remains open to revision by contrary evidence.

A trained thinker judges how much inquiry each situation warrants, rather than applying an inflexible procedure: excessive delay can be as inappropriate as hasty judgment, and past mistakes should improve later thinking.
review_points: Preserve the distinction between generating a suggestion, reasoning from it and checking it against observation.
The five elements are logically distinguished, not five compulsory separate actions in every case.
A successful prediction alone is not presented as unconditional certainty: rival conditions and contrary evidence matter.
Do not expand the three illustrations into the whole summary at the expense of their shared process and practical qualification.

bullets: Reflection moves between particular facts and a possible unifying meaning: induction suggests an explanation, while deduction develops its implications and returns to facts to test, revise or reject it. Neither movement is sufficient alone.
Suggestions cannot be guaranteed by rules, but their formation can be guided indirectly by improving observations, scrutinizing assumptions and keeping proposed explanations provisional.

Scientific inquiry selects relevant evidence through analysis, comparison and contrast, including contrary cases. Mere repetition of similar observations is insufficient; planned experiments make significant conditions more visible and variable when feasible.

Organized principles, definitions and classifications help frame problems and derive consequences worth checking. However plausible the reasoning becomes, concrete observation must test its conclusions.

Teaching should connect facts with explanations, require learners to develop their own suggestions, and apply principles to new cases. The chapter favors opportunities for active experimentation, without requiring elaborate laboratories or treating definitions as ends in themselves.
review_points: Induction is not defined as simply collecting many similar cases; the chapter allows inference within a single case.
Control over the occurrence of suggestions is indirect and imperfect, not a guaranteed recipe for discovery.
Both contrast and comparison matter; do not omit exceptions or turn supportive cases into automatic proof.
The account of deduction includes development and empirical testing, not validation through formal plausibility alone.
Definitions and organized knowledge are tools, not rejected outright.

bullets: Judgment resolves a doubtful situation with competing interpretations by examining evidence and meanings, then reaching a decision that can guide similar future cases. It differs from both immediate recognition and wholly unexplained mystery.

Good judgment selects significant facts rather than merely conspicuous details, while developing and comparing possible interpretations. Experience can build this discernment, but fixed rules or a large stock of information cannot substitute for it.
An idea is a possible meaning held tentatively as a tool for inquiry. Treating it as already certain ends investigation, while retaining it as a testable possibility guides further observation.

Analysis emphasizes relevant features, and synthesis places them in a meaningful context; both cooperate in every judgment rather than functioning as opposed methods or literal mental disassembly and reassembly.

Educational methods should grow through inquiry and later reflection on what worked. Premature demands for explicit formulas, exhaustive lists or ready-made procedures can hinder the development of effective habits of thought.
review_points: Judgment involves reciprocal selection of evidence and interpretation, not reading an importance label already attached to each fact.
The chapter distinguishes a tentative idea used in inquiry from an image or memorized assertion.
Reviewing successful methods is useful; the criticism concerns premature imposed formulation, not all explicit methods.

The source contains an incidental Alice in Wonderland cake allusion; preserve the complete chapter, disclose this overlap, and do not use it in the teacher summary or claim zero phrase overlap with evaluation books.
